@@9627579 <p> If there is a lesson to learn from Brexit it might well be that work and employment will increasingly be the battleground on which arguments about democracy play out , writes Tim Dunlop . <p> As the protean shockwave of disbelief , anger , approval , disapproval , concern , disruption , elation - and any other emotion you care to name - spreads out around the world in the wake of the Brexit vote , it occurred to me , as it probably did to you , that there is something fundamentally wrong with how the world is run . <p> I am less concerned with whether or not it is desirable for Britain to leave the European Union than I am with the fact that the British referendum represents something of a turning point in discussions of democratic governance . <p> Whatever you think of the EU , it is clear that significant sections of the British public , and other member states , feel disenfranchised by an organisation they see as being run by and for the benefit of elites at the expense of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in regard to issues around employment and labour law , and it is worth looking at what is happening . <p> Instead of concentrating on the real reasons for joblessness , unemployment is being managed by xenophobia , with cynical elites shifting the blame onto immigrants . <p> The Brexit referendum is a perfect example of this sort of manipulation . The blunt instrument of a yes-or-no vote was used to determine an issue that shades into almost infinite shards of complexity . A detailed consideration of the facts was replaced by an us-versus-them referendum . <p> ( And we wonder why we end up with confusion rather than clarity . Not to mention hate and violence . ) <p> In the wake of the 2007 global financial crisis , the EU imposed the sort of labour laws on various member nations that Australians would recognise as WorkChoices on steroids . That is , harsh neoliberal measures designed to " discipline " workers in the name of " competitiveness " . <p> Researchers Aristea Koukiadaki , Isabel T ? vora and Miguel Mart ? nez Lucio point out in a paper @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ result of the austerity measures stipulated in loan agreements and/or recommendations issued by the International Monetary Fund ( IMF ) , the European Central Bank ( ECB ) and the European Commission ( EC ) - acting often together as the so-called " troika " - essential features of national labour law and industrial relations systems ... have been , or are in the course of being , radically revised . <p> That is to say , the carrot of financial aid is being disciplined by the stick of changes to labour laws . <p> The report goes on to note that these changes do not " respect the diversity of national systems , including the role ascribed to social partners and the principle of democracy . " In other words , they are not open for debate . <p> There was also a subsection on the wage bargaining framework that included the following " suggestions " : <p> ... cut statutory and contractual minimum wages ; reduce bargaining coverage ; decrease ( automatic ) extension of collective agreements ; " reform " the bargaining system to make it less centralised @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the possibility to derogate from higher level agreements or to negotiate company-level agreements ; promote measures that result in an overall reduction in the wage-setting power of trade unions ... <p> The researchers note that even the European Parliament itself " stressed the possible negative impact of such practices on political stability in the countries concerned and citizens ' trust in democracy and the European project . " <p> Ya think ? <p> Not being part of European Monetary Union , Britain is actually spared from some of these provisions , though the irony is that their own government is imposing a very similar regime . In other words , leaving the EU will make no difference . <p> The point is , problems around work - from the lack of jobs , to the increase in precarious employment , to stagnant and falling wages - are at the core of disaffection around democratic governance . <p> If , as many suggest , we are heading into a period of increased unemployment and insecure work caused by technological advances - robotics , artificial intelligence , 3D printing amongst other things - @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ It means we will have to stop lying to ourselves about the " jobs coming back " and start thinking about ways other than wages to distribute wealth . <p> How is it that in nearly every nation - including the richest and most technologically advanced - there is at this moment in world history , a white-hot core of anger and resentment that is threatening to tear apart the institutions of democracy and governance more generally ? <p> How is it that , at a moment when we are on the brink of some of the most wonderful technological innovations in history , developments that create the prospect of a life of relative ease and prosperity for all , that we seem incapable of grasping those opportunities and instead plunge headlong into division and inequality ? <p> The basic democratic deficit created by the neoliberalism of Europe and most other governments , including our own , is at the heart of it . Technocratic imposition has been prioritised over the hard work of grassroots consensus building . <p> So if there is a key lesson to learn from Brexit it @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ on which arguments about democracy will play out . <p> We either find a way to create the sort of stable jobs that can provide people with a decent standard of living across a lifetime - increasingly unlikely in my view - or we rethink the centrality of work to our societies and find other ways to distribute national wealth . <p> Politicians gave the British voters a crude instrument with which to respond to complex problems and they blew up the European Union and the United Kingdom , destroying trillions of dollars in wealth . <p> That was not the fault of voters , as many are now insisting . The blame lays squarely with generations of politicians who have engineered a system that rewards the few at the expense of the many . <p> How much longer do you think these stupid elites can go on pretending that all this disaffection , this righteous anger , can simply be managed away ? <p> Tim Dunlop writes regularly for The Drum and a number of other publications . He hosts the podcastWashington Dreaming , discussing the forthcoming US Presidential Election @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , will be released in September 2016 . @@9636635 <h> Green and cool roofs provide relief for hot cities , but should be sited carefully <h> Author <h> Disclosure statement <p> Ashish Sharma is affiliated with the Environmental Change Initiative , ND Energy and the Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering and Earth Sciences at the University of Notre Dame . Research described in this article is supported by the National Science Foundation , the Notre Dame Environmental Change Initiative , the Notre Dame Center for Sustainable Energy , and the City of Chicago . <p> More than half of the world 's population lives in cities , and the United Nations projects that this share will rise to 70 percent by 2050 . During the daytime , these expanding urban areas absorb more solar energy than the surrounding countryside . At night they radiate the heat back to the atmosphere . Higher temperatures in cities compared to the areas around them create what are known as urban heat islands ( UHIs ) . <p> In a recent study conducted by the University of Notre Dame 's Environmental Change Initiative , we examined whether green roofs , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ which are surfaced with reflective materials , could reduce UHI effects in Chicago . These roofing strategies are widely used across Europe and have recently been adopted in multiple U.S. cities , including New York , Los Angeles , Chicago and Portland , Oregon . Developing cities in Asia , such as Indore in India are also implementing cool roofs to mitigate UHIs . <p> Post-doctoral researcher Ashish Sharma on a green roof at the Morris Inn , University of Notre Dame , USA.Author provided <p> We found that these roofing strategies did reduce the urban heat island effect , but their impacts were not uniform within the city . They also reduced breezes from Lake Michigan and altered regional air circulation in ways that could offset some of their cooling and air quality benefits . While the roofs still had a net cooling impact , urban planners will need to understand impacts on energy consumption and air quality to maximize benefits from installing green and cool roofs . <h> Why cities are getting hotter <p> The world 's urban areas are rapidly expanding , and the density of city populations @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ million people lived in cities ; in 2014 , that number had risen to 3.9 billion . By 2045 more than 6 billion people may live in urban areas . <p> Urban heating is caused by many factors . They include the properties of building materials such as thermal conductivity , thermal mass and thermal resistance ; air emissions produced by building heating and cooling systems and motor vehicles ; urban designs that trap heat in street canyons , preventing it from radiating back to the atmosphere at night ; and body heat produced by residents themselves . <p> Infrared image showing buildings radiating heat in downtown Chicago <h> How green and cool roofs can help <p> Our research showed that green and cool roofs helped to reduce UHI effects in Chicago . But we also observed important regional- and local-scale effects that affected how well these systems performed . <p> First , the impacts of green and cool roofs on UHIs varied at different locations . We found that green and cool roofing strategies reduced daytime peak urban roof temperatures across the Chicago metropolitan area by about 2-3 degrees Celsius @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ temperatures by 7-8 degrees Celsius . This dramatic difference indicates that green and cool roofs are most efficient in highly urbanized areas . <p> Second , because green and cool roofs lowered rooftop temperatures in the city , they reduced the relative temperature difference between air over Chicago and air over adjoining Lake Michigan , which is typically 4-5 degrees Celsius cooler than air over the city during daytime in summer . By doing so , they weakened the strength of breezes that blow from the lake to the shore in warm weather and help to cool shoreline neighborhoods . Urban planners can offset this effect by designing streets so that they channel air easily instead of blocking natural flow patterns . <p> Third , we found that these rooftop surfaces did not just reduce temperatures immediately above the urban rooftops . Their impact extended into the lower atmosphere , up to altitudes of about 2.5 kilometers . This affected regional weather patterns by reducing local convection -- a process in which warm air rises into the atmosphere , removing heat from earth 's surface . <p> Overall , our analysis @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ actually decrease wind flow in Chicago by lowering horizontal wind speeds and reducing vertical air mixing during daytime . This may lead to air stagnation near ground level , and potentially could reduce air quality . We are investigating these possibilities now . <h> Choosing between green and cool roofs <p> Green and cool roofs each offer advantages and disadvantages . Installed on a large scale , green roofs could add a substantial amount of green space to cities and provide habitat for plants and insects across urban areas . Additionally , plants can improve urban air quality by removing solid and gaseous pollutants from the air . <p> On the other hand , cool roofs do not require watering and cost less than green roofs to install and maintain . Green roofs also increase local humidity : moisture is released when plants are watered , and plants release more water to the atmosphere from their leaves . <p> Many other issues will also influence decisions about where to install green and cool roofs . One important consideration is environmental justice . Low-income and minority neighborhoods are disproportionately vulnerable to negative @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ choose to focus heat reduction strategies on these areas . <p> It is also important to note that human thermal comfort is governed by many variables , including time spent outdoors , social and economic behavior , and access to cooling resources , such as air conditioning and swimming pools . Planners should consider these factors as they apply heat mitigation strategies at the local scale . <p> Getting more insight into the effects of green and cool roofs can inform city planning initiatives , such as the Chicago Wilderness Green Infrastructure 2040 Vision , by identifying where green and cool roofs will work most effectively . Cities in northern latitudes , such as New York , Portland and Toronto , can benefit from green roofs because they have adequate water to irrigate them . In contrast , cool roofs are more appropriate for cities in arid and semi-arid environments such as the southwestern United States . <h> Cities in a warming world <p> In the words of John Wilmoth , director of the United Nations Population Division , " Managing urban areas has become one of the most important development @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ urban population is growing , and climate change will add to urban heating . <p> Unless societies act to mitigate UHIs , rising urban temperatures will threaten human health , strain energy resources , and reduce economic productivity . Green and cool roofs are excellent choices to mitigate urban heat island effects , and can be applied at a city-wide scale or block by block . Together with other strategies -- such as adding more parks , lawns , ponds , trees and other green infrastructure -- they can help to keep temperatures in the world 's cities livable.

@@9645546 <h> Turnbull is home and hosed ? Not so fast <p> It may be this election does go the way of expert consensus : the Turnbull Government returned with a reduced majority . But there 's enough evidence to suggest we should consider the unexpected , writes Mike Steketee . <p> So Malcolm Turnbull has the election in the bag . Home and hosed . Put down the glasses . <p> Well perhaps . Except there has never been a better , dare we say more exciting , time to expect the unexpected . <p> British voters have just ignored the advice of their government , opposition , treasury , central bank and world leaders and taken themselves out of the European Union . American voters have done what pretty well all the experts said was inconceivable and installed Donald Trump as the presumptive Republican nominee for president . <p> Yes , this is Australia , not the UK or the US , and this Saturday we may end up doing what has been the expert consensus for the past few weeks : elect the Turnbull Government with @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ quirky , not to mention peed off , as well ? <p> While there may not be as many signs of wholesale revolt against the major parties , there is deep disillusionment . The Coalition 's primary vote is 39 per cent and Labor 's 37 per cent , according to this week 's Essential poll , meaning a quarter of voters intend to cast a ballot for other parties or independents . And that is just in the lower house . <p> The received wisdom used to be that a party that can not manage 40 per cent of first preference votes can not get elected . But that was on the assumption that one of the major parties would poll higher . <p> Unlike in Britain and other countries where the voter turnout can be critical to the outcome , the major polls in Australia have a fairly good track record for accuracy , thanks mainly to compulsory voting . At least that is the case for the polls measuring the nationwide vote and those that are taken as late as possible , a day or two before the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> Even then voters can have a change of heart at the last minute , as they did in 1993 , when the Keating government defied predictions by winning re-election . But if the most recent poll figures do turn out to be accurate by Saturday , it does not necessarily mean the winning side actually wins . <p> Polling in marginal seats in this election suggests that , although matching the Coalition on the national vote , Labor is not winning enough support in the right seats to gain a majority . These surveys have smaller samples and therefore are not as reliable as the national polls . Nevertheless they are backed up by Labor strategists who are telling journalists that they are falling short . <p> There could be an element of spin in these " confessions " in an attempt by Labor to retain underdog status . <p> The pop psychology logic here is that if people think Labor is going to win they are less likely to vote for it . It does n't work for the Coalition because no-one thinks it is the underdog . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the re-election of the Government . Malcolm Turnbull has been a disappointment to many voters but are they prepared to throw him out at his first attempt at winning government ? For Labor to take 21 seats from a first-term government in order to win an overall majority was always going to be a big challenge . <p> First-term governments have been defeated - more often in recent times . It happened to the Newman government in Queensland and the Napthine government in Victoria . It has not occurred federally since 1931 , during the Great Depression , when the Scullin Labor government lost office , although the Gillard government had a close call in 2010 . <p> But there also is the question of how much precedents count in the current political environment . According to Turnbull , Tony Abbott would have lost this election " resoundingly " if he were still prime minister . Self-serving , perhaps , and not the most tactful comment when he is trying to promote an image of government unity . But on the available evidence , he is right . Not much sentiment @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ more volatile than ever . Tim Colebatch points out that at nine of the last 12 elections in Australia , including those at state and territory level , people voted to throw governments out . ( He has included South Australia in 2014 , where Labor stayed in power contrary to the wishes of the majority of voters . ) The exceptions where governments were re-elected were the ACT in 2012 , Western Australia in 2013 and NSW last year . <p> Brexit is supposed to have swung the election in the Coalition 's favour . But how much are voters listening to Turnbull 's pleas for stability and to elect a government with a clear majority ? Certainly not when it comes to their planned Senate vote . <p> The Australian economy is faring better than many overseas . But with the mining boom well and truly behind us , there are hip pocket issues that have definite potential to influence the way people vote , such as falling real per capita net incomes and unaffordable housing . Pauline Hanson has a good prospect of winning a Senate seat in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a la Donald Trump , including on Muslim immigration . <p> Exactly what is making up the mind of voters is becoming harder to determine , with multiple and diverse messages through social media and activist third party organisations such as GetUp . <p> At the end of a long , typically unenlightening and often unedifying campaign , Turnbull senses that Australians want less ideology and an end to juvenile theatrics and personality politics - in short , a step-up in political culture . We can only live in hope . <p> In the meantime , the fate of government lies in the hands of millions of voters making individual decisions based on a myriad influences in a process that is inherently unpredictable . <p> Mike Steketeeis a freelance journalist . But I do n't claim to understand the details @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 01 Jul 2016 12:55:32pm <p> When there are 12 vacancies the quota for a spot is 7.69% . All first preferences are counted and all candidates with a quota are declared elected . If a candidate has more than a quota their surplus votes are distributed according to a formula . This takes into account that one quota of votes have been used ( eg , a candidate gets two quotas all of his second preferences are distributed at 50% value . In effect , if all are voting down the list it means the second candidate gets elected as well with no surplus to distribute . If at this stage of the count no remaining candidates have a quota then the lowest scoring candidate is eliminated and the next preference of their voters is distributed . Process continues with either the election or elimination of one candidate at each stage until all vacancies are filled . If a significant number of preferences exhaust ( that is possible now with the new system ) and we reach a point where no candidate has a quota but the remaining candidates equal the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Debbie : <p> 01 Jul 2016 10:30:24am <p> Sillyme - it is very complicated and totally different counting system to the House of Reps . @@9646773 <h> Blackstone 's Byron Wien says uncertainty hovers around a new GFC <p> ' The greatest concern is about what would happen if the developed world slipped back into a recession for any reason , ' says Blackstone vice chairman Byron Wien . Louise Kennerley <p> by Byron Wien <p> These are confusing times in both the United States and Europe . The forthcoming US presidential election has two unpopular ( according to the polls ) candidates running against each other . One is viewed as untrustworthy and the other as dangerously extreme . In the UK the " Leave " vote was a shocker . Britain is the second-largest economy in the Union , and its departure creates concern about whether others will follow . Because of that there may be an effort by EU leadership to achieve the separation quickly . Some worry that the EU will punish Britain for its decision , as a warning to other countries considering defection . I hope not . Article 50 of the Lisbon Treaty provides for a two-year period of negotiation of a withdrawal agreement . A work-out @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ even being part of a single market , would be ideal . At this point , Angela Merkel seems to be in favour of a gradual withdrawal . In any case , the " Leave " outcome is a setback for growth in Britain , in Europe and around the world at a time when economies are generally struggling . Not a good sign for markets for the rest of the year . While the vote was decisive , key " Remain " constituents did not turn out as expected . Younger voters were 75 per cent in favour of " Remain " and they had a 36 per cent turnout . Scotland , which favoured " Remain , " had a low turnout . The weather in and around London was bad favouring " Leave " ; older , less-educated rural voters held sway . The overall turnout was a heavy 72 per cent . There is some buyer 's remorse , but it is done . <p> The economic historian Walter Russell Mead , a professor at Bard , believes that Brexit and nationalism generally derive from a systemic @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the Eurozone ; ( b ) the Middle East refugee crisis and fear of terrorism ; and finally ( c ) Russian aggression . In the United States , he sees scepticism toward trade agreements and a growing isolationism . Donald Trump 's ascendency to the Republican nomination is also a reflection of those populist ideas . So is Bernie Sanders ' younger-voter following , which emerged in response to growing inequality and a lack of opportunity . A major common thread in both Europe and the United States is the fear about immigration . On both sides of the Atlantic the average person is concerned about the loss of jobs to immigrants who will be satisfied with lower wages . In Europe there is the additional worry that if Turkey were to become a member of the Union and its people have easy entry into any member country , the flow of immigrants into prosperous nations like Britain would be considerable . <p> The ethnicity issue is central on both sides of the Atlantic . The Orlando shootings by an American-born Muslim did not temper the views held by the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ that the few should not contaminate the many . As expected , Donald Trump believes the incident proves all Muslims should be excluded from entry into the United States . Trump recognises that terrorism has made Americans generally afraid , and therefore is useful politically . Voters who are scared , on either side of the ocean , are likely to act emotionally , which is what made the outcome of the referendum uncertain . While economic issues argued strongly for Britain remaining in the European Union , fear of disruptive immigrants ultimately dominated the thinking of many people . When fear is the controlling factor , fundamentals on the other side of the issue play a smaller role . This will be a consideration in elections across the continent in the coming year . <h> Unlikely fiscal stimulus <p> During June I travelled to London , Amsterdam , Paris , Geneva and Zurich , meeting with investors and discussing the factors that were contributing to asset allocation uncertainty everywhere . I think it is fair to say that Europeans are baffled by the prospect of Donald Trump becoming President of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the world order . While they know that American political leadership can veer off in troublesome directions , they believe that Trump represents a new precedent that they hope can be restrained by Congress if he is elected . The confusion that populism has created on both sides of the Atlantic has made asset allocation decisions difficult for European portfolio managers . I did n't find anyone who was enthusiastic about any asset class . Most were looking for a place to hide until the outlook clarified , but the feeling was that the investment landscape would not improve soon . <p> The greatest concern was about what would happen if the developed world slipped back into a recession for any reason . Everyone was aware that the current expansion began in the middle of 2009 , making it one of the longest on record . If we got into an economic recession on either side of the ocean , what policy steps could be taken to hasten the recovery ? Interest rates are already at record lows and further monetary accommodation might be less productive than previous efforts . Conservative @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ States are not likely to pass legislation providing major fiscal stimulus measures . Central banks dealt with the financial crisis of 2008-09 very effectively , but there is no guarantee that the next crisis will be handled with similar skill . <p> At present , Europeans seem resigned to a prolonged period of slow growth . They are puzzled by the negative interest rates in Germany and Japan but believe there is significant risk aversion among investors who are looking for a place to store their money until they develop more conviction about where they can find capital appreciation opportunities , and some are willing to pay the banks a storage fee to do it . They are also unsettled by the uncertain political outlook on the continent as they look ahead to the numerous elections scheduled over the next year . Angela Merkel has lost political capital at home and with other members of the European Union over the immigration issue , and she was the putative leader of the continent . Europeans have no idea of what to expect after the new leadership takes over in Washington . They @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ unwilling to count on that . <h> Double-digit returns ? <p> Europeans are aware of the importance of monetary expansion in causing the equity markets to rise and keeping interest rates low . They wonder what will happen to the US economy when the Fed starts shrinking its balance sheet back to more normal levels . It has $US4.5 trillion in bonds on its books now ; back in 2008 it had $US1 trillion . In my discussions , I pointed out that a serious reduction of the Fed balance sheet was unlikely to happen soon , because the economy is vulnerable to any form of monetary tightening . <p> Everywhere I went , investors pleaded with me to suggest an asset class where they could get double-digit returns . When I told them that future nominal returns from public equities were more likely to be closer to 5 per cent than 10 per cent , they were disappointed but understood my reasoning . If world real growth were 2 per cent and inflation were 2 per cent and productivity were 1 per cent , 5 per cent is all you @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ number of discussions about productivity . I suggested that we needed to see productivity of about 1 per cent for profits to improve and the standard of living to rise . Currently we are running at about half that rate . Many believe that the measurement process does not pick up the contributions to productivity that have come from technology . One pointed out that in Europe the underground or " black " economy plays an important role , and its output data is not picked up in the productivity figures . <p> The general thinking in Europe is that growth is slow but okay . Youth unemployment is still high , but real GDP growth for the continent should still be 1 per cent for 2016 . The refugee crisis is under control for the moment and some jobs are being created . The problem may be in part a result of the European Union becoming too big , with too many countries and no strong central leadership . The bureaucracy is cumbersome and costly and the regulatory framework has become a burden . Consequently , companies are always looking @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ is a prime option . In this climate of uncertainty , many people are attracted to candidates with extreme positions , but so far the outsiders are not yet in control . <h> Wanting more opportunity <p> Europeans are very worried about political instability in the Middle East leading to a rise in the price of oil . Some believe that the recent rise carries a supply disruption premium . They say oil can not be looked at as a simple supply/demand problem . Terrorism and regime change in key countries has to be taken into account . Some thought the enthusiasm about energy was unfounded . The price may stay lower than expected because of fracking and increased production from Iran . Many Swiss investors are buying gold again . Several believed there were opportunities in Africa but were reluctant to make investments there . One pointed out that the German work force is shrinking faster than the Japanese . Since Germany is the prime mover in European growth , this is a serious concern for the future . <p> One investor said market volatility and a lack of discernible trends discouraged him . Another noted that the mobility advantage would always favour America . Europeans have a language problem that limits moving , and they have difficulty selling their houses . @@9646822 <h> Antarctic ozone hole has finally started to heal , scientists report <h> Chris Mooney <p> In a major new paper in the influential journal Science , a team of researchers report strikingly good news about a 30-year old environmental problem . <p> The Antarctic ozone " hole " - which , when it was first identified in the mid-1980s , focused public attention like few other pieces of environmental news - has begun , in their words , finally to heal . <p> " If you use the medical analogy , first the patient was getting worse and worse , and then the patient is stabilised , and now , the really encouraging thing , is that the patient is really starting to get better , " said MIT atmospheric scientist Susan Solomon , lead author of the study , and former co-chair of the United Nations ' Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change . <p> The ozone hole over Antarctica in 2006 . Photo : NASA <p> Moreover , that patient - the Earth 's vital ozone layer - is getting better directly because of our choices @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ sudden discovery of a vast seasonal ozone " hole " over Antarctica in 1985 that the world was shocked into action . <p> The so-called " hole " represents a region of the stratosphere over Antarctica , between about 10 and 25 kilometres in altitude , where " the ozone gets destroyed completely " , Solomon said . <p> However , some ozone remains above and below this region , amounting to a 40 or 50 per cent loss of atmospheric ozone overall in a very large area of air . <p> Ozone has been depleted in the stratosphere all across the globe . But Antarctica in the southern hemisphere spring presents uniquely conducive conditions for it to happen , as extremely cold polar stratospheric clouds provide a surface that enables the chemical reactions in which destructive forms of chlorine to be created . <p> Discovery of the " hole " galvanised action and , in 1987 , the Montreal Protocol , which is still today hailed as the epitome of a successful environmental agreement , led to a phase-out of the use of ozone depleting chemicals . <p> Here was @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ story of climate change , because everything basically functioned as it was supposed to - scientists identified a problem , the public grew concerned , and politicians acted to solve it . <p> " You have to put yourself back in the time when the ozone hole was discovered , " Solomon , who has been studying the issue for more than three decades , said . <p> " We thought we were going to see a few per cent change in the ozone layer in a century . And then all of a sudden , boom , we 've got half as much ozone in a part of the world where nobody ever expected it , already happening in 1986 . It became a tremendous hot environmental crisis as a result of that . " <p> Ever since the Montreal Protocol was adopted , it has been a process of waiting for ozone depletion in the atmosphere to slow down , then for decline to cease entirely , and then , finally , to see the ozone layer turn the corner and begin to grow back . And it is @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ozone hole in particular , the new study asserts . <p> In the research , the researchers used satellite and balloon data to examine the seasonal Antarctic ozone hole for a 15-year period between 2000 and 2015 . And they found that , in September , the size of the hole had generally declined by more than 3.9 million square kilometres , and that this was a trend that could be statistically separated from the " noise " of natural variations . <p> " The September size of the ozone hole shows this very systematic trend of getting smaller , and the September measurements also show that the ozone has begun to recover just exactly in the height range where the polar stratospheric clouds are , " she said . <p> The study also found that " roughly half " of the improvement seen in September was " chemical " in nature , or , in other words , the result of fewer ozone-depleting chemicals in the stratosphere . <p> October , the peak month for Antarctic ozone depletion , is another matter . October 2015 actually showed a quite large @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ size , it was 28 million square kilometres . <p> But another part of the new study is to explain why October remains a highly variable month for ozone depletion over Antarctica - one in which it is hard to detect a healing signal - and why last October was so bad , even as the ozone hole is clearly healing . And the answer is volcanoes - specifically , the eruption of a volcano named Calbuco in Chile . <p> Large volcanic eruptions fill the stratosphere with sulfur dioxide and , depending on where they occur , this can circulate around much of the globe . <p> Southern hemisphere eruptions spread sulfate across that hemisphere , Solomon said , and the sulfur dioxide aids in the formation of polar stratospheric clouds , once again enhancing ozone depletion . <p> The study used a climate model to simulate how volcanic contributions enhanced the ozone hole in October . <p> Therefore , the paper was able to conclude that one bad October did not detract from an overall , if slow , early ozone recovery . <p> Granted , there is a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ October ozone hole over Antarctica will still be with us until about 2050 and , depending on volcano behaviour , there could be more setbacks and large swings along the way . <p> Still , it 's hard to interpret the current paper as anything other than a piece of ( rare ) good news when it comes to the interactions between humans and their planet . And it tempts one to think bigger about its broader significance . <p> The ozone issue and the climate issue have long been conjoined , not merely because they are both problems involving the global atmospheric commons , or because chlorofluorocarbons are also greenhouse gases , but also because they emerged into public consciousness about the same time . <p> This can be seen in a historic 1986 hearing before Congress in which scientists not only raised early climate alarms , but paired those with presentations about ozone depletion and the Antarctic hole . However , the world went on to solve one of the problems before too much damage set in - but has failed to do nearly as well with the other @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , is less than clear . On the pessimistic side , one could say that the contrast proves that a modest-sized global environmental problem can be solved by the world , while a mega-sized one is another matter entirely . <p> " On the scale of things this was a different type of problem , " Solomon said . " It was an industry measured in the billions , not the trillions . " <p> Yet she said the evidence that the Antarctic ozone hole was finally getting better made her optimistic about our capacity ultimately to come to grips with climate change as well . <p> " Technology and innovation can do miraculous things , " she said . " We still have airconditioners , we still have refrigerators , we still have hair spray . We did n't have to give up much , and yet we got to a state in which the atmosphere is much better off , and we 're better off . "
